description: Hire Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2024.

talks.title: Inverting the Corporate Interview to Get You Hired
talks.teaser: Explains how behavioral interviews are judged and how candidates can prepare stories and answers that stand out.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who has spent roughly 26 years hiring software developers and other technical staff, opens by arguing that interviews favor the employer. Companies chasing operational efficiency want low salaries, so the process can be built to leave candidates off balance, and many interviewers receive little training. Understanding that context helps a candidate see why the process feels the way it does.

The middle of the talk explains behavioral interviewing, which assumes core competencies are stable and that past behavior from roughly the last five years predicts future behavior. Interviewers therefore ask for specific stories and probe for details, since detail makes fabrication harder. Preparation advice includes collecting stories with input from coworkers, practicing answers aloud, writing notes by hand, and learning about the panel beforehand. Candidates should also have answers ready for "tell me about yourself" and "greatest weakness," and should keep the phone off and arrive early on the day.

The closing portion covers whether to challenge the team's process or fit in. The speaker advises against an offensive posture, warning that it can trigger a hiring manager's defenses, and recommends being confident without being cocky. The practical takeaway is to prepare concrete, memorable evidence of skills and deliver it calmly.

talks.title: You Need a Jay-z and a Beyoncé
talks.teaser: Explains how sponsors and mentors differ and how each one helps advance a cybersecurity career.
talks.summary:
Anthony Hendricks, a cybersecurity and data privacy attorney, uses Jay-Z's 2024 Grammys speech about Beyoncé as a way into a career question: what a sponsor does that a mentor does not. He separates the two roles. A mentor offers encouragement, advice and perspective, and may be an older senior colleague, a peer who has already faced the same problems, or someone who reflects your strengths back to you. A sponsor spends their own influence to advocate for a protégé, puts them forward for stretch assignments, shields them from criticism, and signals to others that they are worth backing.

The middle of the talk draws on business research. It cites a Harvard Business School experiment at a call center where a structured four-week mentoring program improved new hires' revenue and retention, and a corporate sponsorship program that moved many participants into larger roles within a year. The speaker notes that many sponsors do not understand their role well, that people often confuse the two terms, and uses a former Xerox CEO's account to show how air cover works in practice.

The closing section gives practical steps. Seek mentors widely, since they are easier to find, and earn a sponsor by delivering results and researching their priorities. Bring value back, be punctual, state your goals clearly, and agree on expectations early. The main takeaway is that both relationships matter, and that isolation and burnout are real costs when they are missing.

talks.title: Brute Force Your Job Application
talks.teaser: Explores a brute-force, high-volume approach to searching for and applying to jobs.

talks.title: What Goes Bump in the Night? Recruiter Panel About Job Search and Other Scary Things
talks.teaser: A recruiter panel discusses the job search and other tricky parts of finding work.

talks.title: Tracking and hacking your career
talks.teaser: Shows how to turn a company's career ladder into a development plan and make your work visible for promotions.
talks.summary:
Leif Dreizler, an engineering manager, argues that career growth works best as a collaborative plan rather than something employees wait for a manager to hand over. The session aims at individual contributors, though he says managers can apply the same skills. He explains how performance reviews and calibration shape ratings, pay and promotion, and why people should learn how these work at their own company before review season.

The middle of the talk covers day-to-day habits. He recommends keeping a running list of accomplishments, writing brief weekly notes about colleagues, and keeping design docs and project retrospectives as evidence. Impact should be framed in business terms, ideally with metrics. He then shows how to turn a company's career ladder into a deconstructed development plan, rated row by row, with the employee and manager filling it in separately before comparing. He also describes promotion theses, which set out why now, the case for promotion and the case against it.

He closes by urging listeners to own their development, document progress and setbacks, and prepare for manager or team changes by keeping clear project records. Making work visible through demos, team channels, blogs and talks is presented as part of getting recognized, not bragging.

talks.title: How Living and Quilting History made me a better Cybersecurity Professional
talks.teaser: Shows how lessons from living history and quilt appraisal carry over into day-to-day cybersecurity work.
talks.summary:
Mea Clift, who works as a cybersecurity engineering adviser in the insurance sector, uses this Hire Ground session to argue that skills from hobbies can sharpen professional judgment. Her background includes years of portraying 18th and 19th century figures, collecting and appraising antique quilts, and restoring sewing machines. She frames the talk as a set of stories, each tied to a lesson she carried into security work.

Several lessons come up. Primary sources matter: a family pension file showed an ancestor had served only six days, undercutting the praise he had received locally, so unverified claims should be checked against evidence. Folklore needs care too. A popular myth about patients biting lead bullets during surgery turned out to rest on a misreading of animal teeth marks, and a scare over Wi-Fi toothbrushes showed how fear can stall useful action. Seeing the whole picture is another point, since a monitoring tool alone does not complete an OT security program. Legacy systems also persist, with a 1975 PLC and old Windows versions still in use, so old and new must be managed together.

The closing message is that practitioners should explain risk in relatable terms, read their audience, and keep learning. Clift encourages listeners to look for connections between their own interests and their work.

talks.title: How to Succeed in a Role that Didn’t Exist
talks.teaser: Offers practical lessons for taking on a newly created security role, from proving its value to building the right alliances.
talks.summary:
Munish Walther-Puri talks about what it takes to succeed when hired into a security role that did not exist before. He describes these positions as "pirate unicorns": exciting and unconstrained, but often viewed by the existing organization as either a threat or an invasive species. The opening explains how to recognize a genuinely new role by asking what prompted its creation, why now, who sponsored it, and whether the organization has created such roles before.

The middle of the talk covers common pitfalls. He recommends identifying internal customers in the first 90 days, testing hypotheses about who needs the role, and asking people who say an approach will not work what they tried and what they learned. He suggests mapping stakeholders as allies, adversaries and potential recruits, and explaining the role's value in terms other teams already care about. He stresses humility and humor as ways to ease an outsider's entry. Examples come from city government, critical infrastructure, fraud and threat intelligence work.

He closes by urging newcomers to define success early, rely on a sponsor and a group of advocates, and build on earlier efforts rather than starting from scratch. He points to a book on first-90-day transitions as a practical reference. The talk is aimed at people who are in, or are considering, a newly created role.

talks.title: Penetration Testing Experience and How to Get It
talks.teaser: Shows newcomers how to gain penetration testing experience through labs, bug bounties, CVEs and networking.
talks.summary:
Phillip Wylie, co-author of The Pentester Blueprint, opens with his own route into offensive security: professional wrestling, jewelry sales, a trade school for AutoCAD, and a move from systems administration into application security and then a first pentest role. He argues that career changers should not wait for a job title before building skills, since hands-on work from earlier roles transfers well.

The middle of the talk focuses on building practical experience. He recommends getting comfortable with vulnerability scanners such as Nessus alongside manual testing, using Kali Linux and Windows-based toolkits, and working through Metasploit, Burp Suite and ZAP. He suggests home labs, CTF platforms, bug bounty programs, low-cost or pro bono assessments for small organizations, and pentest-as-a-service contracts as ways to log real work. Publishing CVEs found in open-source software, writing walkthroughs, and sharing code on GitHub are presented as ways to show employers what you can do.

The closing section covers networking and job search tactics: attending BSides and local hacker and ISSA meetings, keeping an active LinkedIn profile, and asking contacts for referrals. He cautions against paying for mentorship and against generic certification roadmaps, favoring practitioner-recommended credentials and red-team courses as next steps.
